job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
For our explainer ahead of next Thursday's markup, we want to cover the bill's weak spots. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — single-vessel threshold.** The definition covers recovery of *more than* 10,000 metric tons per year by a single vessel. Operators could stay at or below that threshold, or split recovery across vessels, and argue their activity is not “commercial deep seabed mining.”

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — uncertain scope and measurement.** “Other mineral resources,” “recovery,” and the period over which annual tonnage is measured are not defined. That leaves room to dispute what materials or activities count and how the threshold applies.

3. **Section 2(1)(B) — discretionary, undefined test.** The Secretary may bring other activities within the definition if they pose “comparable” ecosystem risks, but the bill sets no criteria or process for that determination. Until the Secretary acts, operators could argue an activity is outside the prohibition.

4. **Section 2(2) — narrow definition of “U.S. person.”** It includes citizens and corporations organized under state law, but not expressly U.S. residents, partnerships, LLCs, or other entities. Those actors—and foreign-organized subsidiaries of U.S. companies—could argue they are not covered as U.S. persons abroad.

5. **Section 2(3) — narrow “covered vessel” definition.** The registry applies only to vessels over 5,000 gross tons that are “equipped” for recovery. Smaller vessels, vessels below that tonnage, or equipment whose purpose is disputed could fall outside the registry requirement.

6. **Section 3(a) — gaps in who and what the prohibition reaches.** The ban applies to a “person in the United States” or a defined “U.S. person” anywhere, but neither term’s application is spelled out for entities, conduct involving U.S. territory, or foreign operations with U.S. links. “Engage in” is also undefined, leaving uncertainty about whether financing, transporting, processing, purchasing, or assisting mining is prohibited.

7. **Section 3(b) — broad grandfathering.** The exception covers mining “conducted under” any exploration license issued before enactment, without limiting the exception to exploration, setting an end date, or requiring a particular license standard. An operator could argue that commercial mining remains protected if it is conducted under a pre-enactment exploration license.

8. **Section 3(c) — open-ended assessment exception.** The bill does not define “environmental assessment” or require approval, limits on extraction, or independent oversight. An operator could characterize mining as assessment activity, potentially allowing recovery that would otherwise be prohibited.

9. **Section 4(a) — registry does not cover all potentially relevant actors.** Only operators of “covered vessels” must register, and the bill does not define “operator.” Owners, contractors, or operators using smaller or differently configured vessels may avoid registration or dispute who bears the duty.

10. **Section 4(b) — limited and underspecified reporting.** Reports describe recovery activities, but the bill does not specify what information they must include, when quarterly reports are due, or how NOAA can verify them. The requirement reaches only registered operators and provides no express consequence for missing, inaccurate, or incomplete reports.

11. **Section 5 — weak enforcement framework.** The bill specifies penalties for violating section 3 but does not expressly authorize an agency or the Attorney General to investigate, bring enforcement actions, seek injunctions, or seize equipment. It also gives no explicit penalty for violating the registry or reporting requirements.

12. **Section 5(a) — penalty uncertainty.** A civil penalty of “not more than” $1 million per day leaves the amount to discretion, with no factors or process specified in the bill. The provision also does not clarify how separate violations or continuing conduct should be counted.

13. **Section 5(b) — unclear criminal standard.** The bill does not define “willfully,” leaving room to dispute what knowledge or intent prosecutors must prove. That uncertainty could make criminal enforcement harder.

14. **Section 6 — no guarantee of international restrictions.** The Secretary must only “seek to negotiate” an agreement, with no requirement that negotiations succeed, that an agreement be concluded, or that Congress receive progress reports. The provision therefore does not itself constrain foreign actors outside section 3’s reach.

15. **Section 7(a) — uncertain end-of-prohibition process.** Ending the prohibition depends on a joint resolution after a National Academies report, but the bill sets no deadline or procedure for the report and does not specify what findings it must contain. A joint resolution also requires enactment through the ordinary legislative process, so it is not a simple automatic administrative off-ramp.

16. **Section 7(b) — conflict with the duration provision.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition remains in effect until Congress makes a finding, while subsection (b) says the entire Act ceases to have effect after 10 years. The bill does not say which rule controls if Congress has not acted by then, creating uncertainty about whether the prohibition automatically ends.

17. **Section 8 and Section 5(a) — conflicting start dates.** The Act takes effect 180 days after enactment, but civil penalties expressly apply to violations occurring “on or after” enactment. That could be read to impose penalties during a period when the prohibition is not yet effective.
